1cb0b41065cb7013: Gadi Eisenkot or Benjamin Netanyahu – under whose direction will Israel head? Erik Marmor/picture alliance via Getty ImagesThe Israeli election of Oct. 27, 2026, was among the most highly anticipated votes in the country’s history. It was consequential, if not yet conclusive. With nearly all the votes counted, it is still unclear who will lead the country following the first national ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, and the devastating wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that Israel has launched since. The Conversation turned to Dov Waxman, an expert on Israeli politics at the University of California, Los Angeles, to walk us through the main takeaways and the process and difficulties facing anyone trying to form a coalition government following a divided vote. What can we take away from the election results? The first thing to note is simply the massive turnout – with a 77.7% turnout of those eligible voting, the highest turnout in more than two decades. That in itself is significant. It underscores how much importance Israelis attached to this vote. Before the election, many observers were saying that it was one of the most consequential – if not the most consequential – votes, and clearly many Israelis felt the same way. What drove this high turnout was different types of fears. Israelis of all persuasions were worried about how the outcome would affect what kind of country Israel becomes. The second big takeaway is that the ruling coalition, formed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the 2022 election, was resoundingly rejected by the majority of Israeli voters – well over 50% cast their vote for parties opposed to the current government. Likud supporters at an election night event in Jerusalem, Israel. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images The five parties that make up Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious coalition went into the election with 68 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That same bloc will now have 53 – and that is a significant loss, no matter how Netanyahu tries to spin this as a victory. It means that those five parties will not be able to form the next government, and as such, the vote stands as a repudiation of the Netanyahu government. Netanyahu’s Likud party will still be the largest in parliament. But its share of the national vote declined, and it looks like it will have six fewer seats in the next parliament, another blow to Netanyahu. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners fared worse than expected, too. In part, this was due to “wasted votes” going to a new far-right party that failed to make it above the 3.25% of the national vote needed to be represented in parliament. Also, Likud drew some voters away from these far-right parties who had voted for them in the last election. What drove the Arab parties’ surprise showing? The performance of the Arab majority parties – the more secular and left-wing Joint List and the more religious and conservative United Arab List – is very important. Combined, they currently look to have increased their representation by nine seats, bringing their total to 19, a historic high for them. The reason for that is the massive turnout of Arab voters – much higher than the last election. But also, a less noticed trend is the increase in Jewish votes that those parties received. It is important to note that these are Arab-majority parties, not simply Arab parties. Israeli left-wing protesters call for the formation of a government including Arab parties. Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images Aside from Netanyahu, it was also a disappointing result for the main opposition party, Yashar; its leader, Gadi Eisenkot; and the anti-Netanyahu Change Bloc it was part of. The preelection polls suggested that the Zionist opposition bloc would do slightly better than the ruling coalition bloc. But Yashar ended up with over 200,000 fewer votes than Likud, winning a projected 21 seats compared to Likud’s 26, and the “Change Bloc” is heading to 48 seats, far short of a parliamentary majority. Ultimately, what is clear is that the Israeli public remains deeply divided. And the fact that there is still a good chance that Netanyahu will emerge as prime minister is remarkable given that many observers had already written his political obituary after the Oct. 7 attack. Was the vote a referendum on Netanyahu? Certainly many saw this as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only person to be trusted with Israel’s security, especially given the threat from Iran. They credit him for weakening – albeit not defeating – the two non-state actors that most threaten Israeli security, Hezbollah and Hamas, and they praise him for ensuring President Donald Trump’s support for Israel. But for those who voted against Netanyahu, the fact that he has refused to take any personal responsibility for the Oct. 7 security failure – amid reports that he had advance warning of a major planned Hamas attack – factored into his poor election showing, as did his government’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 security failings. Many also blame Netanyahu for not prioritizing the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza and prolonging the war there. He is also held responsible by many for the precipitous decline in Israel’s international standing and for jeopardizing Israel’s crucial alliance with the United States. But it was domestic issues, rather than external ones, that motivated many of those who voted for anti-Netanyahu parties. Many fear that democracy in Israel is under attack, and they particularly oppose the effort by Netanyahu’s government to weaken the power and independence of the Israeli judiciary, which sparked massive street protests in 2023. They also strongly resent that Netanyahu’s government has allowed ultra-Orthodox men to avoid military service, despite the Israeli military’s growing manpower shortage. And on a personal level, Netanyahu is widely perceived as self-serving and dishonest – he is still on trial for corruption. Arab voters have other, more specific concerns that drove them to vote in record numbers, in addition to the Netanyahu government’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank, which they strongly oppose. Chief among them is the soaring rates of violent crime in their communities, which the government – particularly the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police – has done nothing to address, say his critics. More broadly, many Palestinian-Arab citizens of Israel fear that if the far-right parties remained in power, their civil rights would be under threat. What should we expect next? The key thing to underline is what happens on election day in Israel is just the first stage in the process of forming a new government. Since no party ever receives a majority of seats in the parliament, what really matters is what happens after the election when the coalition building begins. This can take weeks, if not longer. The party with the largest number of seats typically gets the first chance to assemble a governing coalition, but not always. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will choose who gets the first chance to form a government based on who is most likely to succeed. Right now, it looks like Eisenkot will get the first opportunity, but his only real option is to form a minority government that would depend on the parliamentary support of the Arab-majority parties – which some members of his Change Bloc adamantly oppose. Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves an Israeli flag as he addresses supporters on Oct. 28, 2026. Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images Despite the success of the Arab-majority parties in the election, it is unlikely they will be invited to be formal members of any coalition – although that has happened once in the past, when the United Arab List joined the short-lived government of 2021-22 led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. If Eisenkot is unable to form a government, then Netanyahu will get the chance. He could try to entice some leaders of the parties in the Change bloc to defect and join a right-wing government under his leadership, or a broader “national unity” government with a rotating leader. Netanyahu did that in the past with Benny Gantz, but then he later prevented Gantz from becoming prime minister – so I doubt Eisenkot would agree to do this with Netanyahu. There are reports in the media that the Trump administration would like a national unity government in Israel, so that might increase the pressure on Eisenkot to accept this outcome. And should war with Iran heat up again, that would increase the pressure. The most likely scenario, I believe, is that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot will be able to form a government, and a new election will be called, with Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister until that vote. Netanyahu has reason to hope that his bloc will do better in another election, so that may well be his game plan. In which case, it will be many months until Israel has a new government. 05fbd3b81be964a0: From Martin Vengadesan
I couldn’t help but be struck by the contrasting leadership styles on display in the run-up to the Melaka polls.
While neither is a candidate for chief minister, both PKR’s Adam Adli and Umno’s Dr Akmal Saleh are the faces of the future for their respective parties.
To me, Adam of PKR displays a soft-spoken, progressive style. There is backbone to his principles, and he was a student leader who was detained and harassed by the previous regime.
He chose to join a multiracial party and has progressed from PKR Youth chief to deputy minister of higher education after winning the Hang Tuah Jaya parliamentary seat.
While he often comes under the cosh over the failed PTPTN loan abolition, I have seen him at work trying to extend the benefits of our nation to its less fortunate.
On the other hand, there’s the rabble-rousing Akmal of Umno. The two men were born a year apart but represent very different ways of thinking.
Indeed, his career reads to me like a hall of shame. But presumably, it has some appeal among the rempit crowd.

Just last week came another defamation suit loss, as the Melaka High Court ruled in Teresa Kok’s favour over his September 2024 remarks slamming her for questioning a proposed mandatory halal certification.
Kok was awarded RM250,000 in general and aggravated damages, plus RM50,000 in costs. He had called her an “old Nyonya” and suggested placing a non-halal logo on her forehead.

Now he says he is prepared to give up his bid to defend the Merlimau state seat in the Melaka election on Nov 14 if the court case he faces over a charge under Section 505(b) of the Penal Code hurts Umno and Barisan Nasional’s chances at the polls.
Akmal is charged with making statements on his Facebook page that allegedly caused public fear, alarm, or disruption to public order.
The charge stems from a viral Facebook video and post made around Aug 11, 2025, regarding an incident in which the Jalur Gemilang was displayed upside down.
Akmal said he had conveyed his position to Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, stressing that the party’s interests must come before his personal ambitions.
This is, of course, merely the latest transgression by a man who has positioned himself as an ethnic champion. Akmal was also previously involved in a defamation suit brought by his sibling.

In 2024, he called on the prime minister to sack tourism, arts and culture minister Tiong King Sing after bak kut teh was recognised as a national heritage food. In the same year, he was involved in a dispute over vernacular schools that led to an insinuation that his opponent, P Ramasamy, was drunk.
And of course he led the KK Mart boycott campaign after socks bearing the word “Allah” were discovered on sale there. Is his brand of politics toxic or constructive? I leave you to decide.

Adam has been working quietly to build consensus. The fact that he cares about all Malaysians does not make him any less of a member of his race or religion. In fact, that is one of the great false assumptions in Malaysian public life.
In his roles at the higher education ministry and the youth and sports ministry, Adam has supported several public-facing initiatives, including PTPTN loan repayment flexibility.

Under the repayment measures announced in the 2027 budget, borrowers earning between RM2,501 and RM3,000 a month are required to make minimum monthly payments of RM50, while those earning below RM2,500 a month are eligible for repayment exemptions.

Other initiatives for students include support for transit passes like My50 and MyKomuter50, alongside the FlySiswa flight subsidy of RM500 for students who travel between Peninsular Malaysia and East Malaysia.
He has promoted technical and vocational education and training (TVET) to bolster graduate employability and supported the revival of the Rakan Muda programme for youth development.
He has also been involved in local infrastructure and welfare projects in Hang Tuah Jaya, such as local flood mitigation.
More than anything else, he views the future with a keen mind and open heart. These are the leaders we need if we are to stop going around in circles.
Martin Vengadesan is a former editor who currently serves as a strategic communications consultant to the communications ministry.

270aee5ea45a14da: Melihat senarai calon wanita untuk PRN Melaka saya sebetulnya terkedu. Ia cepat membawa saya kepada watak-watak wanita ikonik dalam sejarah Kesultanan Melayu Melaka. Sukar untuk memadam watak-watak seperti Tun Kudu, Tun Teja dan Tun Fatimah dari benak. Malangnya wanita yang saya sebutkan ini dihinjak dalam politik.

Ambil sahaja Tun Kudu yang menjadi sekadar 'alat' untuk kepentingan penguasa. Tun Kudu adalah puteri kepada Bendahara Seri Wak Raja dan merupakan permaisuri kepada Sultan Muzaffar Syah yang memerintah Melaka (1446-1459). Namun demikian untuk meredakan perseteruan dua kem politik orang Melayu yang berebutkan kedudukan sebagai bendahara, Sultan Muzzafar Syah telah menceraikan Tun Kudu dan mengaturkan baginda untuk menjadi isteri Bendahara Seri Nara Diraja yang sudah tua kerepot, lagi berusia.

Seri Nara Diraja memang menyebabkan Sultan Muzaffar sakit kepala kerana enggan bersara, membolot jawatan tersebut setelah Bendahara Seri Wak Raja dan hanya sedia melakukannya dengan syarat diberi hadiah gundik sultan. Makanya dalam percaturan Sultan Muzaffar, Paduka Raja Tun Perak, iaitu kekanda Tun Kudu terpaksa mengambil sikap damai. Tun Ali atau Seri Nara Diraja itu adalah bapa saudara Sultan Muzaffar Syah dan pembesar yang bertanggungjawab mengatur dan meletakkan Sultan Muzaffar di atas takhta pada 1446.

Watak kedua pula adalah Tun Teja iaitu anak Bendahara Pahang Seri Amar Bangsa Diraja dan disebut sebagai tunangan kepada Sultan Pahang, Sultan Abdul Jalil. Akan tetapi Sultan Mahmud Syah yang gila perempuan telah berusaha mendapatkan Tun Teja lantas bertitah kepada pembesar; "Barang siapa membawa anak Bendahara Pahang itu ke mari, apa yang dikehendakinya ku anugerahkan akan dia. Jikalau ia hendakkan sekerat kota dengan kerajaan sekalipun kita anugerahkan".

Dalam riwayat, Tun Teja dilarikan oleh Hang Nadim (menantu kepada Laksamana Hang Tuah) demi menebus kesalahannya terhadap sultan. Untuk melakukannya, Hang Nadim merasuah seorang pelulut untuk memujuk Tun Teja agar kelak berkahwin dengan Sultan Mahmud Syah. Berdasarkan Hikayat Hang Tuah, Tun Teja merupakan seorang yang bermaruah tinggi dan bukanlah gilakan kedudukan. Beliau malah menolak lamaran sultan Melaka, sebaliknya memilih menjadi isteri Megat Panji Alam Terengganu.
Perbuatan pelulut membujuk Tun Teja ini gagal. Oleh sebab Tun Teja liat dan berkeras, malangnya baginda disihir dengan ubat guna-guna lantas dipaksa berkahwin dengan Sultan Mahmud tanpa kerelaan.

Sultan Mahmud Syah selaku raja dan sultan yang gila perempuan seterusnya mensasarkan pula Tun Fatimah. Baginda adalah anak Tun Mutahir dan baru berkahwin dengan Tun Ali. Sultan Mahmud Syah menggunakan kuasa baginda untuk membunuh Tun Ali sebelum merebut Tun Fatimah. Ini juga didorong oleh fitnah Raja Mendaliar kononnya Tun Mutahir sedang merancang untuk menggulingkannya. Sultan menitahkan Tun Sura Diraja dan Tun Indera Segara untuk menghabisi seisi keluarga bendahara. Kesan atau trauma kehilangan seisi keluarga dan suami itu, Tun Fatimah hidup berendam dendam. Dalam riwayat disebut Tun Fatimah itu 'selama ia duduk dengan Sultan Mahmud Syah jangankan ia tertawa, tersenyum pun tiada pernah'. Bahkan setiap kali mengandung, baginda menggugurkan kandungannya.

Kisah raja gila seks, termakan fitnah dan pertelingkahan politik antara kem pembesar untuk berebut kedudukan dan jawatan bendahara ini adalah satu renungan yang penting untuk kita memahami pula konteks semasa.

Hari ini Melaka menyaksikan sekali lagi perebutan kuasa dalam bentuk pilihan raya. Dengan mengambil ingatan, Melaka melayan watak wanita sebagai alat percaturan politik, pemuas nafsu dan sekadar di pinggiran; saya dengan berhati-hati mencari parti politik yang tidak melakukan hal-hal sedemikian. Saya juga menyuruhkan kaum keluarga saya yang terdiri dari pengundi wanita untuk tidak memilih mereka yang melayan wanita dengan buruk.

Sudah tentu kita telah menjauhi era kesultanan Melayu yang penuh malapetaka seperti di atas. Iklim politik kita juga harapnya tidaklah setoksik itu. Pun tenung punya tenung saya mesti memastikan parti politik manakah yang tidak menjadikan wanita sekadar melukut di tepi gantang. Saya benci perlakuan Melaka di zaman lampau tersebut.

Mengapakah saya memberi tumpuan kepada wanita? Jawapan mudahnya, ini adalah kerana dalam rekod, terdapat 348,849 orang pengundi di PRN Melaka kali ini adalah perempuan, iaitu 50.73% daripada jumlah keseluruhan pemilih. Justeru saya berpandangan penting untuk kita melihat komponen parti manakah yang paling bersungguh memperjuangkan wanita.

Letak duduk wanita dalam politik adalah penting terutama setelah ucapan kontroversi di Persidangan Agung Umno 2026, iaitu apabila Presiden Zahid Hamidi berseloroh mengatakan Ketua Wanita Noraini Ahmad nampak macam 'nenek-nenek'.

Pakatan Harapan menjanjikan lima orang calon wanita untuk membawa mandat rakyat Melaka di kawasan masing-masing. Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) mengetengahkan tiga orang calon wanita dalam PRN Melaka, pada 14 November ini. Menurut Setiausaha Agung Fuziah Salleh, daripada sembilan calon yang diketengahkan parti itu, tiga calon wanita telah diberi kepercayaan untuk bertanding, dan ini mewakili 33.3% daripada keseluruhan calon PKR pada PRN. Calon wanita ini adalah Ketua Pemuda Tangga Batu, Farzana Hayani Nasir di Klebang; Ketua Penerangan Wanita Ginie Lim Siew Lin yang sekali lagi bertanding di DUN Machap Jaya, dan Esma Eazreen Husin di Rim. Farzana, seorang Gen Z baru-baru ini mendapat perhatian ramai apabila diusir seorang anggota wanita Umno dari menghadiri program Kampung Angkat Madani di kawasan masjid Bukit Rambai.

Dalam pada itu, Amanah di Merlimau membawakan Rahayu Hamzah. Beliau akan membawa tugas besar untuk menewaskan Ketua Pemuda Umno, Dr Akmal Saleh yang baru-baru ini kalah dalam saman berkaitan isu cadangan pensijilan halal, di mana Akmal merujuk Ahli Parlimen Seputeh, Teresa Kok sebagai 'nyonya tua'. Akmal diperintahkan membayar ganti rugi berjumlah RM250,000 kepada Teresa. Ini termasuklah kos perundangan sebanyak RM50,000 (jumlah keseluruhan RM300,000). bea6ae276ae0bb55: When a child refuses to share a table with another child because one eats pork, we are no longer talking about a minor classroom incident. We are talking about a failure of national education.
Malaysia’s schools are now producing children who see difference as contamination, faith as a barrier, and fellow Malaysians as people to be avoided.
This is not unity. It is segregation being taught early, quietly and dangerously.
A warning from the classroom

Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin recently revealed that some primary school pupils had refused to sit beside classmates of another faith. Among the reasons were that a classmate was eating pork or wearing a cross.
Let that sink in.
Children young enough to still be learning multiplication tables are already being taught, directly or indirectly, that another child’s food, religion or symbol makes them unworthy of friendship.
Do not hide behind the excuse that “children repeat what they hear at home”. Of course, families matter.
But schools are where society either corrects prejudice or normalises it. If a child can carry such intolerance into a classroom without being firmly challenged, then the classroom has failed.
Unity cannot remain a slogan
For decades, Malaysia has recited the Rukun Negara, held unity-themed assemblies and printed national slogans on walls, banners and exercise books.
Yet what is the value of a national principle if a child will not sit beside another child because of what that child eats or believes?

The Rukun Negara is not decoration. It is not a mural. It is not a slogan for official events. If it means anything, it must be visible in how children treat one another every day, in classrooms, canteens, playgrounds and school buses.
Our education system has become too comfortable with symbolism. It celebrates diversity on stage but often fails to build genuine relationships across communities in daily school life.
Separate childhoods, divided futures
Malaysia’s national, Chinese and Tamil primary schools reflect our multicultural reality. Preserving mother tongues and cultural identity is legitimate and necessary.
But preserving identity must not mean raising children in social isolation.

When pupils spend their formative years largely among those who look, pray, eat and speak like them, anything different becomes unfamiliar. And unfamiliarity easily induces fear. Fear becomes prejudice. Prejudice breeds rejection.
How can we expect adults to build a united Malaysia if, as children, they were never given real opportunities to know one another?

Joint sports, debates, arts, science projects, community service and shared classrooms must not be occasional photo opportunities. They must be routine, structured and compulsory parts of school life, not pleasing politicians for their occasional visit to school.
Stop pretending the system is fair
We must also stop pretending that education policy is neutral.
For too long, access to opportunities, scholarships, school placements and pathways has been viewed through racial lenses.
Whatever the original intention, the consequence is clear: many young Malaysians grow up believing that their future depends more on their ethnicity than their effort, talent or need.

Helping the disadvantaged is right. But assistance must be transparent, needs-based and accountable. A system that leaves one community feeling privileged and another feeling excluded cannot claim to be building unity.
A child who believes the system does not value them equally will not easily believe the nation values them equally.
Malaysia built on community effort

Our history lessons must stop being exercises in memorising dates and names. They must teach the harder truth: Malaysia was built through negotiation, compromise and cooperation among communities that did not always share the same faith, language or customs.
Tunku Abdul Rahman, Tun Tan Siew Sin and Tun VT Sambanthan came from different communities, yet they worked towards one national objective: independence.
If our founding leaders could sit at the same table and build a nation, why should a child today refuse to sit beside a classmate because of pork or a cross?
No community owns Malaysia. Every community helped build it. Every community has a stake in protecting it.
The education ministry must answer
This is not a problem to be passed to the national unity ministry while the education ministry (MoE) hides behind curriculum documents.
The MoE must answer directly:
Why are children absorbing religious intolerance in schools?
Are teachers trained to identify and confront prejudice early?
Are schools required to create meaningful interaction across communities?
Are incidents of discrimination investigated, recorded and corrected?
Are school leaders held accountable when unity exists only in speeches?
If the ministry cannot enforce the values it preaches, then it is not merely failing pupils. It is failing Malaysia.
Make unity measurable
National unity must become part of every subject, every school and every level of education.
Kindergartens must teach children to play, share and cooperate across backgrounds. Primary and secondary schools must run regular joint programmes with schools of different streams.
History, literature and civics must teach shared nationhood, not narrow narratives. Group work must deliberately bring children out of familiar ethnic and religious circles.

Teachers need training in inclusive classroom practices, religious literacy and conflict resolution. Textbook writers must be held accountable for accuracy, balance and the removal of stereotypes, not mere focus on any one community.
And the ministry must publish measurable indicators: pupils’ sense of belonging, participation in cross-community activities, teacher preparedness, complaints handled and corrective action taken.
Unity must be assessed, not merely announced.
The future is sitting in our classrooms
A child who refuses to share a table today may become an adult who refuses to share a country tomorrow.
This is the harsh truth Malaysia must face: our education system is not merely underperforming academically; it is failing in its duty to mould Malaysians.

We can continue producing students with excellent grades but shallow citizenship. Or we can rebuild schools into places where children learn that faith, food, language and culture must never determine who deserves their friendship.
Malaysia’s future will not be decided only in parliament or boardrooms. It will be decided at classroom tables, where children either learn to see one another as strangers, or as fellow Malaysians.

d29f179e903a044f: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

b8365cf2bf687c78: In the first round of the 2026 Brazilian presidential election, on Oct. 4, the politics of resentment prevailed. Frustration among those displaced from their jobs by automation and the newly self-employed – who sometimes wrongly see themselves as “entrepreneurs” – fueled the vote for the opposition of Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and favored far right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. In the runoff on Oct. 25, however, the driving motivation shifted from resentment to fear of a return of the so-called “Bolsonarismo” to power. President Lula was reelected in a second round whose outcome could hardly have been anticipated from his lackluster first round campaign and Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead of 2.2 million votes. So what changed? First, Lula took his campaign to the streets, where it had been largely absent in the first round. And it also moved into social media, where Lula’s presence had preiviously amounted to little more than a translation of analog campaigning into digital formats. Another important factor was the fear generated by Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round lead. Until then, there had been a widespread conviction – not only among Lula and his campaign team, but throughout democratic society in general – that the president would be reelected. A change in attitudes The shock with the results of the first round, followed by fear of a far right victory, brought about a change in attitudes and a spontaneous mobilization in the streets, beginning with students in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro state and spreading to large and medium sized cities across the country. Fear intensified as Flávio Bolsonaro increasingly revealed his resemblance to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for attempting a coup after losing his bid for reelection in 2022.. In the 27 state capitals and 162 other major Brazilian cities, encompassing nearly 75 million voters – close to 47% of the total – Lula’s gains were decisive, according to a survey by news and data analysis website Dado Bruto. He won in 13 of the state capitals, including São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. In Minas Gerais, he lost in capital Belo Horizonte, although he carried the state. Overall, in the state capitals, Lula gained 2.2 million votes in the runoff, offsetting Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round advantage. Across the 189 Brazilian major cities, Lula’s vote share rose by nearly 3.5 percentage points. This result helped him make gains in every state. He reversed the first round defeat in Minas Gerais, improving his performance in the second round by more than three percentage points. Urban Brazil delivered Lula’s victory. He won in 12 states in the first round, and in 13 in the second. Consider Osasco, a major city in the state of São Paulo, whose GDP is overwhelmingly generated by the service industry, particularly finance, technology, logistics, and ecommerce. The city has nearly 729,000 inhabitants and a GDP per capita of R$ 164,000 (US$30,000). Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round in Osasco by 191,700 votes to Lula’s 182,700. In the runoff, Lula reversed the result, winning by 234,300 votes to 213,200. In many of these major cities, voters took to the streets in support of Lula. On social media, the extensive reach of the WhatsApp network “Exército do Lula” – or “Lula’s Army” –, with more than 10 million followers and managed by reelected congressman André Janones, certainly had a significant positive effect in generating additional votes for the president. The interaction between digital networks and street mobilization played a decisive, if not determining, role in his reelection. In the major cities of agribusiness strongholds, Flávio Bolsonaro won more than 70% of the runoff vote. A particularly representative municipality is Sinop, in the state of Mato Grosso, where he won the first round by 73,700 votes to Lula’s 17,500. In the runoff, Lula gained another 4,700 votes, while the Liberal Party candidate added 3,800, making little difference to the final result: 77,500 votes to 22,200, with Flávio Bolsonaro winning 77.7% of the votes. Urban-rural cleavage revived The expansion of export oriented agribusiness, particularly in Brazil’s center-west and north regions, but also in the South and the north-central and northwestern regions of Minas Gerais, has revived the urban-rural cleavage of Brazilian politics. This divide was at the heart of the most serious political and electoral conflicts of Brazil’s Second Republic, from 1945 to 1964. During that period, the troubled relationship between an executive branch elected by urban Brazil and a legislature whose majority was elected by rural Brazil produced legislative paralysis, contributing to the breakdown of democratic institutions that led to the 1964 coup. Today, although the rural economy is technologically advanced, this divide has taken the radicalized form of political polarization, destabilizing the political system and threatening the country’s governability. It generates an authoritarian impulse that materialized under Jair Bolsonaro’s administration. Jair Bolsonaro was convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup and is serving his sentence. The prosecution and conviction of those involved in the attempted coup have dispelled neither radicalized polarization nor the authoritarian impulse. The latter resurfaced unmistakably in Flávio Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept the clean and democratic verdict of the ballot box. It was precisely this persistent coup oriented impulse that made the runoff mobilization possible, through a clearly visible interaction between digital networks and the streets. The decline in voter alienation, which brought 4.8 million electors back into the pool of valid votes, vividly expresses this reaction driven by fear of a return to Bolsonaro’s attempts to overthrow democratic institutions. Nearly 2.9 million additional voters turned out at the polls. Invalid votes fell from 3.7 million to 2.7 million, while blank ballots declined from 2.3 million to 1.4 million. Voter alienation dropped by three percentage points. The future of Lula’s fourth term This coup oriented impulse is particularly important when we consider the composition of the newly elected Brazilian Congress. A majority of those elected to Congress in the first round are sided with Flávio Bolsonaro. Beginning in 2027, President Lula’s room for maneuver in Congress will be narrower. In both the House of Deputies and the Senate, it will be possible to assemble a majority coalition, but one in which the center-right and right will carry greater weight. Members of the “Centrão”, Brazil’s parties known for their transactional politics, are inclined to align themselves with those in power by definition. In the House, the moderate right and the Centrão together would account for approximately 66% of a possible Lula’s coalition’s votes, and in the Senate, 56%. This would significantly alter the configuration of Lula’s fourth administration, which would rest on a broad democratic coalition, but not a progressive one. Lula intends to add digital mobilization to his presidential toolkit, drawing on the experience of “Lula’s Army”. The objective would be to raise Lula’s public approval ratings, thereby strengthening his ability to negotiate with and exert pressure on Congress. Anyway, the president would have to open up his administration further and become more receptive to parties outside his traditional political and partisan circles. This fourth term will mark the end of the Lula era. After this cycle, Brazilian politics will have to change, renew its leadership, and take into account the emerging generation of digital politicians. The end of this era also coincides with the departure from the political stage of the generation that resisted the military dictatorship that took power in 1964, from which three Brazilian presidents emerged: Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Lula, and Dilma Rousseff. Generational succession is inescapable. Brazil’s new generation of politicians will be more attuned to digital society. 071e826394b5b671: For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated. Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world. The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century? In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum, which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin. Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different? A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers. Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids.  What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure. If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon. This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more possibilities, much faster and at a lower cost.  But the story of that hasn't been written yet, and the outcomes could still be very positive, depending on what we do. Q: Can you give an example of infrastructure systems becoming more interconnected in a way that changes how we build or manage them? A: The revolution in information technology and digital transformation over the past 30 years has made infrastructure systems more interconnected. You see this in cities. If the power goes out, water and gas systems can stop functioning, internet fails, and transportation system comes to a halt. If communications networks fail, many other services are affected. We saw this during Covid, when disruptions in supply chains affected energy networks, critical materials, and manufacturing. We see it when geopolitical conflicts disrupt oil and energy markets and those disruptions propagate through other parts of the global economy. Infrastructure systems that were once managed separately are increasingly dependent on one another. As we connect more things together for more efficiency, we also increase systemic risk and expose the systems to rare but catastrophic failures. They have become rare, but when they happen, they're much bigger and more consequential. The really tricky thing is that developing infrastructure involves much more than designing and building it. The whole value chain includes financing and operating it, as well as understanding who will use it and what those users need and prefer. So, designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult. There’s also so much uncertainty in large infrastructure projects. They’re very capital-intensive, the business is lower margin than many other industries, and projects take a long time. Combine all of that, and it has historically made the industry very conservative. But the transformations coming from AI and digital transformation are potentially offering a new way forward. What that new way looks like, no one has quite delineated it yet. Q: How are you and your colleagues working to change how these decisions get made?   A: We realized that if we're going to develop a new approach to infrastructure, no single discipline, company, or country can do it alone. Infrastructure value chain is too interconnected, and the challenges are too large. That's why MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering co-founded the World Infrastructure Forum with the World Bank Group, the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and University of Texas at Austin. The goal is to bring together academia, industry, governments, and financial institutions across the infrastructure value chain and create an ongoing dialogue about how infrastructure should be designed, financed, built, and operated in the decades ahead. This is particularly important because the biggest opportunities for new infrastructure development are not necessarily in the United States or other countries with mature infrastructure systems. Those countries still face significant needs for modernization and new investment. But over the coming decades, much of the world's population growth, and much of the infrastructure that will need to be built, will be in countries where infrastructure systems are still developing.  Those countries have an opportunity to benefit from modern infrastructure without simply repeating the model of the 20th century. But capturing that opportunity will require new approaches to technology, financing, engineering, and governance. We're trying to create an ecosystem rather than just a forum, a mechanism for continuing the conversation among the different stakeholders across the infrastructure value chain. We've established five working groups and an advisory group of more than 30 leaders from across the infrastructure value chain, including engineering and construction, materials, finance, multilateral institutions, and academia. Ultimately, the question is not whether we need a new way of developing infrastructure. The question is how we create it and who is going to execute it. There is no single person, company, or country that can solve this problem, because infrastructure itself is interconnected. We need to build the new model together.

All images via Canva or fair use. Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube. International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0. St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience. But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function. Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.

Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning. Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better. It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential. Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced. When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business. When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital. When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes. When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

fdc9c053616efe5d: You've probably heard, at this point, about the big changes coming to Meta's AI scraping terms for business accounts. Nieman Lab had that scoop, and since then, small businesses, journalists, and artists using Meta products like Instagram have been raising the alarm. But if you're in the EU or UK, you might be in luck and can object to that use of your data, as some users have pointed out.
If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. On mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objections were approved.
On the podcast this week, we talk Flock CEO’s leaked police conference audio and Sam’s piece about Marissa Mayer’s latest meltdown. Subscribe wherever you get your pods.

The New York Times has an antisocial aversion to linking: Another day, another the-New-York-Times-isn’t-linking controversy. The specifics here almost don’t matter because this happens seemingly every day, but basically the New York Times investigation about chemical plant polluters under the Trump administration was covered in much the same way by Hunterbrook, a news outlet fused with a hedge fund. The Times article—which led the Sunday print edition—uses similar photos, some of the same sources, and covers similar ground to Hunterbrook’s earlier investigation from February, with no acknowledgment or link whatsoever. After the cofounder of Hunterbrook rightfully ranted about this on X, the Times added an acknowledgment (but no link!!!) toward the bottom of the story. Puck’s Dylan Byers has a good rundown about what happened, which includes parts of a three-paragraph Times’ spokesperson statement explaining at length why they don’t think they have to link. This is extremely antisocial, deranged behavior and it’s ridiculous that the Times is still getting away with this. Bottom line: I’m sure the Times was already working on this story, what with their massive newsroom. Even so, they got beat, and they should link. Journalism awards need to stop looking the other way when big outlets do this. This has happened to us many times and it actually does matter for smaller outlets and links are free. Let’s try them!

Artificial reef: TIL that a gigantic military ship, the SS United, is going to be purposefully sunk to be turned into an “artificial reef.” Scuba divers seem quite excited. I didn’t really know that this was a thing that was done, but maybe I’m a rube.

The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. b65bd78dcb9b0242: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

EU users’ personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act. GDPR, which became enforceable in 2018, requires explicit consent to use personal data. This includes the right to object to one’s data being used. The AI Act, which went into effect in 2024, dictates how AI companies can use personal data, and how people can opt in or out, stating that they can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. The European Commission states: “The GDPR rules only apply to personal data about individuals; they do not govern data about companies or any other legal entities. However, information in relation to companies may constitute personal data where it allows the identification of a natural person.”

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. Instagram user bookish.sil posted a walkthrough of how they did it on mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. Instagram user jenniqueart posted a similar walkthrough with the same results.

My Meta accounts are based in the US, but using a VPN to locate my IP address in London, I could see options in my Meta privacy settings that would let me object to the use of my information by Meta AI. To get there on desktop with a VPN on, I went to my account privacy center, clicked “Submit a privacy rights request” at the bottom, selected Instagram, clicked “How can I object to the processing of my information?” and got to a page where I could choose to object to the use of my information for Meta AI or third parties, which were two separate options.
When my location is based in the US, these options don't appear.

When I clicked through the option to “object to the use of my information for Meta AI,” however, it returned an error page that said “This form is only available to people in certain regions.” GDPR is meant to apply to wherever someone is located at the time, but since this objection applies to the preferences of one account, it might be based on where the account was created. I tried again located in Belgium and got the same results. I’ve asked Meta to clarify.

As many have already pointed out in the comments on UK and EU users who’ve posted walkthroughs, these objection steps aren’t available to people outside of those countries, and as Meta continuously changes its platform, these steps might not work for everyone always. Unless something changes before November 20, the rest of us are screwed.
c11769620a3fa457: Security is the dominant feature of the EU's new Arctic strategy. dotshock / ShutterstockThe EU recently presented its latest Arctic strategy. It is the bloc’s fifth such strategy since 2008 and the first to be published since 2021, a few months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This conflict has disrupted Arctic governance. The work of the Arctic Council, which includes Russia as one of its eight member states, was paused shortly after the invasion. The council is the primary forum for cooperation in the region. Since 2022, the Russian security threat in the Arctic has also grown. Russia has engaged in hybrid activities in the region, ranging from disinformation operations and GPS jamming to the targeting of pipelines and undersea cables. The EU’s new strategy has four priorities: strengthening peace, security and resilience in the Arctic, addressing climate change, delivering economic development and ensuring regional and social development for Arctic communities. These priorities are broadly in line with the previous 2021 strategy, in which geopolitical issues were already more present than in earlier years. But there are several major changes. More security and less climate action A word count reveals the profound impact the deteriorating cooperation context has had on the EU’s stance on the region. In the latest update, the word “security” is mentioned 52 times compared with 23 times in 2021. By contrast, “climate change” appears only 14 times in the new strategy compared with 30 times previously. This shift towards security is a general trend in the Arctic since 2022. The creation of an annual Arctic Security Conference in 2024, which discusses security trends in the region, is an example of this. Security also figures prominently in recently published national Arctic strategies, including France, Italy, Germany and Sweden. Climate change is not completely absent from the EU’s latest Arctic strategy, and the bloc reaffirmed its commitment to combat it in the document. But, where previously climate change was the cornerstone of the EU’s Arctic engagement, it is now presented through a security lens. Climate change is identified as “amplifying security risks” and a “defining threat” from which Arctic inhabitants need to be “protected”. Security shapes all four priorities of the new strategy. Arctic communities also get much more attention than in earlier documents. Although the inclusion of Indigenous people also figures more prominently, the conflation between Indigenous and local people has previously been criticised by the Saami Council. The conflation undermines the specific rights and distinct interests of Indigenous groups such as the Sámi. A ‘northern neighbourhood’ Another key change in the EU’s new Arctic strategy is the introduction of the concept of a “northern neighbourhood”. The name suggests similarities with the EU’s European Neighbourhood Policy, which it launched in 2004 to foster closer ties with its eastern and southern neighbours. But it is unclear what exact form the northern neighbourhood will take. The northern neighbourhood is not presented as a new multilateral institution. Instead, it has been put forward as a political framework enabling cooperation projects and integration between the EU and “like-minded” partners such as Greenland, Norway, Iceland, Canada and the UK. By excluding Russia, this new political framework signals a change in the EU’s understanding of the Arctic. The EU’s early engagement in the region came from a will to extend European integration to the east and north in the 2000s. The Arctic was also an area where cooperation with Russia was possible, despite disagreements elsewhere. The concept of a northern neighbourhood reveals a geographical shift in focus towards Greenland and the west and north Atlantic more generally. Yet while the US is still listed among the potential members of the northern neighbourhood, it comes with implicit conditions. According to the new strategy, a partnership with the US needs to be “predictable” and based on “shared interests and values”. This is reminiscent of the language that prevailed for Russia in the previous policies. What kind of power is the EU? Perhaps the biggest change in the new strategy lies in the document’s affirmation that multilateral cooperation “can no longer be the sole foundation of the EU’s Arctic approach”. This means two things. First, that multilateralism is no longer the prominent form of cooperation in the Arctic. And second, that the EU’s geopolitical stance in general is changing from being the champion and embodiment of multilateralism to another form of power. This is also visible in the emphasis the new strategy puts on the EU’s material capabilities and infrastructures as conditions for security. It includes mention of, among other things, developing Europe’s capacity to build icebreaker vessels. The EU’s new Arctic strategy signals a broad shift in the European geopolitical mindset. Climate change and multilateralism have been overshadowed by security concerns due to the fractured Arctic geopolitical landscape. However, ultimately, climate change and social concerns will remain key priorities of Arctic inhabitants and the EU should not lose sight of this. ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. 1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest.
